event-title.$: ENTRY INTO FORCE OF REQUEST FOR SUBSTANTIVE EXAMINATION

section.content: 本公开提供“改进的机器学习”。一种系统包括：图像传感器，所述图像传感器具有车辆外部的视野；所述车辆中的人机界面(HMI)，所述HMI被布置为基于来自所述图像传感器的数据来显示图像；和第一计算机，所述第一计算机包括处理器和存储器。所述第一计算机被编程为将来自所述图像传感器的数据提供给机器学习程序，所述机器学习程序输出围绕对象的边界框；使得围绕所述对象的所述边界框经由所述HMI显示；以及将包括识别所述对象的输入的标签的对象数据传输到远离所述车辆的第二计算机。

The present disclosure provides "improved machine learning. A system comprising: an image sensor having a field of view external to the vehicle; a human-machine interface (HMI) in the vehicle arranged to display an image based on data from the image sensor; and a first computer comprising a processor and a memory. The first computer programmed to provide data from the image sensor to a machine learning program that outputs a bounding box around an object; causing the bounding box surrounding the object to be displayed via the HMI; and transmitting object data including the tag identifying the input of the object to a second computer remote from the vehicle.

Improved machine learningTechnical Field

The present disclosure relates to improved machine learning.

Background

A computer executing a trained machine learning program may use data from image sensors such as optical cameras and lidar to detect and identify objects. The object data may be used for various machines such as vehicles, manufacturing robots, warehouse robots, and the like. For example, data from an image sensor in the vehicle may be provided to a vehicle computer, which may detect and/or identify objects based on a machine learning program, whereby the computer is assisted in controlling and/or assisting vehicle operation. Training machine learning programs to detect and identify objects typically requires a large amount of training data, and may require a large amount of computer processing cycles and time.

Disclosure of Invention

Training a machine learning procedure for object detection and/or recognition relies on a very large number of correctly labeled images, i.e., image data accompanied by labels or tags that specify objects represented in the image data. Advantageously, as disclosed herein, a large number of labeled image datasets may be obtained, and in addition, processing such as cross-validation of the received labeled image datasets may be performed, thereby providing a reliable labeled image dataset for training DNN. As explained further below, a computer in a movable object detection platform, such as a vehicle, may detect an object, which may then be presented to a user via a display in a vehicle Human Machine Interface (HMI). The user can provide a tag for the displayed object via input to the HMI. The user-provided labels and associated image data may then be provided to a central server for use in training a machine learning program such as a Deep Neural Network (DNN). DNNs may then be deployed to, for example, vehicles to provide object detection, which may be provided as a basis for operating machines such as vehicles.

A system comprising: an image sensor having a field of view external to the vehicle; a Human Machine Interface (HMI) in the vehicle arranged to display an image based on data from the image sensor; and a first computer comprising a processor and a memory. The first computer programmed to provide data from the image sensor to a machine learning program that outputs a bounding box around an object; causing the bounding box surrounding the object to be displayed via the HMI; and transmitting object data including the tag identifying the input of the object to a second computer remote from the vehicle.

The machine learning program may also output one or more candidate tags for the object, and the first computer may be programmed to receive input specifying a user selection of one of the one or more candidate tags.

The object may be a first object of a plurality of objects and the bounding box is a first bounding box of a plurality of bounding boxes. The machine learning program may also output the plurality of bounding boxes, including the first bounding box and at least one second bounding box. Each of the bounding boxes may then be provided around a respective object of the plurality of objects including the first object and at least one second object.

The object data may further include data regarding an environment around the vehicle associated with a time at which the input tag was input.

The data from the image sensor may include a plurality of video frames that include the object and are captured during a time interval when the vehicle is moving. The input tag may be a first input tag and associated with a first time in a time interval, and the object data may include one or more second input tags respectively associated with one or more second times in the time interval.

The vehicle may be a first vehicle of a plurality of vehicles and the object data may be a first object data set of a plurality of object data sets, whereby the input tag is one of a plurality of input tags in the respective object data set. The system may also include the second computer, where the second computer includes a second processor and a second memory and is programmed to receive the plurality of object data sets from respective ones of the plurality of vehicles. The second computer may also be programmed to perform cross-validation to validate or reject tags in one or more of the object data sets. The second computer may also be programmed to remove rejected tags from the object data. The second computer may also be programmed to provide an updated data collection program by adjusting rules for requesting user input based on the results of the cross-validation; and providing the updated data collection program to the vehicle. The second computer may also be programmed to classify a user associated with one of the object data sets based on the results of the cross-validation; wherein the rule specifies whether the user is allowed to provide the input data, and adjusting the rule comprises determining that the user is not allowed to provide the input data. The second computer may also be programmed to determine a type of one of the objects in the object dataset, wherein when a candidate tag specifies the type, the rule specifies a frequency of requesting that input be provided to a user providing the input tag for the one of the objects, and adjusting the rule includes adjusting the machine learning program to present the type of object to the user providing the input tag more frequently or less frequently based on a result of the cross-validation. The second computer may also be programmed to compare a respective input tag with map data to perform a verification of one of the input tag or the map data.

The machine learning program can be a first machine learning program, and the second computer can be further programmed to generate a second machine learning program based on the plurality of object data sets to perform object recognition. The second computer may also be programmed to provide the second machine learning program to one or more of the plurality of vehicles or another vehicle. The first computer may also be programmed to receive the second machine learning program and operate the vehicle based on the object identification output from the second machine learning program.

Drawings

FIG. 1 is a block diagram of an exemplary object detection system.

FIG. 2 illustrates an exemplary human machine interface in a vehicle.

FIG. 3 shows another example of a human machine interface in a vehicle.

FIG. 4 is a block diagram of an exemplary deep neural network.

FIG. 5 is a process flow diagram of an exemplary process for training and deploying an object detection module.

Fig. 6 is a process flow diagram including details of collecting data for the training object detection module and the training object detection module.

Detailed Description

Referring to fig. 1, an object detection system 100 may include a plurality of object detection platforms, i.e., mobile machines including elements such as those discussed herein, whereby the platforms may obtain image data at a plurality of locations. The exemplary object detection platform shown and discussed herein is a conventional ground vehicle 102. As shown in fig. 1, a vehicle 102 may include various elements, including a vehicle 102 computer 104 arranged to communicate with other vehicle 102 components, including sensors, various vehicle subsystems 110, and a communication module 120, via a vehicle network 106. Further, fig. 1 shows a plurality of vehicles 102 that may include the various elements described herein, but for ease of illustration, fig. 1 details the various elements with respect to only one of the depicted vehicles 102.

The vehicle 102 generally includes a plurality of computing devices, including a vehicle 102 computer 104 configured to perform object detection operations. The vehicle 102 computer 104 may include various program modules, i.e., computer programs that are sets of program instructions for executing specified operations or algorithms, such as those described below. For example, to support object detection operations, the computer 104 may include a data collection module 122 and/or an object detection module 124.

The data collection module 122 may include a first machine learning program trained to identify candidate objects 132 and possibly candidate tags 136 that may be presented to a user, for example, in the HMI 118 of the vehicle 102, as described further below. The object data collected in the data collection module 122 may be provided to the remote server 128 to train a second machine learning procedure, which may be included in the object detection module 124, which object detection module 124 may be deployed to one or more vehicles 102 to perform object recognition. As shown in fig. 1, the vehicle 102 includes both the collection module 122 and the detection module 124, but in actual implementations, the vehicle 102 may include the collection module 122 without the detection module 124 or include the detection module 124 without the collection module 122. Once trained, the detection module 124 may be provided (e.g., downloaded from a remote server 128) to one or more vehicles 102. The vehicle 102 computer 104 may receive the object detection module 124 including the second machine learning program and may then operate the vehicle 102 according to the object identification output from the second machine learning program.

The data collection module 122 can include program instructions to receive image data from one or more image sensors 108 in the vehicle 102 via the vehicle network 106 and cause the HMI 118 to display the image. The computer 104 may also include program instructions to provide data from the image sensor to a machine learning program included in the data collection module 122 that detects the object and outputs a bounding box 134 of the object that may be displayed around the object. For example, the computer 104 may also be programmed to then display a bounding box 134 surrounding the object via the HMI 118. Via the HMI 118, the computer 104 can receive user input to tag an object (i.e., a tag that the computer 104 can receive input). The machine learning program in the data collection module 122 may be a DNN 138 such as described further below.

The detection module 124 may include a second machine learning program trained to recognize (or classify) objects to support operation of the vehicle 102. For example, the second machine learning procedure may include DNN 138 trained to accept image data as input (i.e., input image data) and output object classifications or identifications, as described below. The second machine learning procedure in the detection module 124 need not be, but may be, trained at least in part using data provided from the collection module 122 in the respective vehicle 102.

An image sensor 108 for providing image data to be input to the data collection module 122 and/or the detection module 124 is included in or on the vehicle 102 and has a field of view external to the vehicle 102. Based on image data from one or more image sensors provided to the computer via the vehicle network, the collection module may identify candidate 132. The candidate object is defined by a set of pixels in the image that are identified by a machine learning program included in the collection module 122 as belonging to the object.

The HMI 118 may include one or more of a display, a touch screen display, a microphone, a speaker, and the like. Alternatively or additionally, the display of the HMI 118 may include an Augmented Reality (AR) display, e.g., to display images and data as described herein in the vehicle 102, e.g., the HMI may include a Heads Up Display (HUD) or the like to display content on a window or windshield (windshield) or the like of the vehicle 102. The user may provide input to a device, such as the computer 104, via the HMI 118. The HMI 118 may communicate with the computer 104 via the vehicle network 106, e.g., the HMI 118 may send messages to the computer 104 including user input provided via a touch screen, microphone, camera capturing gestures, etc., and/or may display output, e.g., via a screen, speaker, etc.

Accordingly, the HMI 118 disposed in the vehicle 102 may be arranged to display an image, including the candidate object 132, based on data from the image sensor. Further, in some implementations, the computer 104 causes the HMI 118 to display a candidate tag 136 for the candidate object 132. In addition to determining objects and bounding boxes 134 of objects in the image data, the machine learning program may output candidate labels 136. The computer 104 may be programmed to receive an input specifying a user selection of one of the one or more candidate tags 136 in response to a list provided via the HMI 118 and/or by a user, for example, via a voice input (e.g., "car" or "tree"), in response to an image including the bounding box 134. In some implementations, the machine learning program may not output and/or the HMI 118 may not display the candidate tag 136. Further, whether or not the HMI 118 displays the candidate tag 136, the computer 104 can also be programmed to receive user input, such as voice input, of the candidate tag 136 via the HMI 118.

In some implementations, the machine learning program can detect multiple objects (i.e., two or more) in the image and can provide a respective bounding box 134 for each of the detected objects. The user may then select one of the objects for tagging and may then provide a candidate tag 136 as described above. For example, in such an example, the two candidates 132 shown in fig. 2 and 3, respectively, may be presented together to the user on the display. The user may select one of the objects, for example, by input to a touch screen or voice input (e.g., "mark left" or "mark right"), and may then provide a candidate tag 136 as just described.

The collection module 122 in the vehicle 102 computer 104 also typically includes programming for transmitting the object data (i.e., the image of the candidate tag 136 including the object and associated input) to the second computer 104 (i.e., to the remote server 128 via the wide area network 126). Alternatively or additionally, the object data may be obtained from the vehicle 102 computer 104 via other suitable mechanisms, for example, accessed through a data port provided on the vehicle 102, such as a USB (universal serial bus) port.

In one implementation, in addition to the image data and the input candidate tag 136, the object data may also include environmental data associated with the time at which the input candidate tag 136 was input; the environmental data is data that provides measurements of phenomena external to the vehicle 102 (i.e., in the environment surrounding the vehicle 102). Thus, the vehicle environment data may include road data, weather data, traffic density data, and the like. Further, environmental data is typically collected by the vehicle 102 sensors 108, but may alternatively or additionally be provided from a source external to the vehicle 102 (e.g., a remote source such as the server 128) based on one or more times the vehicle 102 is at or traveling through a specified location.

The image sensor may include a plurality of video frames that include objects and are captured during time intervals when the vehicle 102 is moving. In such examples, the image of the object presented to the user via the HMI 118 of the vehicle 102 may be a still image, e.g., one of the frames. However, the object data provided to the remote server 128 may include a plurality of frames, for example, frames that last for a period of time (such as 5 seconds, 10 seconds, etc.), as well as the input candidate tag 136. Providing multiple frames collected during a time interval and including objects associated with the input candidate label 136 advantageously provides a richer set of label data than a set of label data available from a single frame (i.e., a frame including objects at a single point in time) for training a machine learning procedure for object identification.

The input candidate tag 136 may be the first input candidate tag 136 associated with a first time in the time interval; the object data may then include one or more second input candidate tags 136 respectively associated with one or more second times in the time interval. That is, the entered candidate tags 136 may be associated with different time intervals. For example, an image of the object may be displayed via the HMI 118 after a first time interval and a candidate tag 136 input by the user may be obtained. An image of the object may then be displayed via the HMI 118 after a second time interval and a second user-entered candidate tag 136 for the object may be obtained. The respective object data sets (i.e., for each of the first and second time intervals) may then be provided to the remote server 128 and stored in the server 128 or in an object database 130 accessible by the server 128.

As described above, the object detection system 100 generally includes a plurality of vehicles 102. Thus, for convenience, the object detection data provided to the remote server 128 from the first vehicle 102 may be referred to as a first object data set of the plurality of object data sets. The input candidate tag 136 included in the first object data set is one of a plurality of input candidate tags 136 in the object data set from respective ones of the plurality of vehicles 102. Accordingly, the central server 128 may be programmed to receive a plurality of object data sets from respective ones of the plurality of vehicles 102.

The server 128 may be programmed to perform cross-validation according to any suitable cross-validation technique to validate or reject tags in one or more of the subject data sets. One advantage of receiving data from multiple vehicles 102 and/or from multiple users is that cross-validation can be used to evaluate input from the respective vehicles 102 and/or users. For example, object data may be collected from multiple vehicles 102 and determined to be related to the same object, i.e., object data is collected at respective locations within a predetermined threshold (e.g., five or 10 meters) of each other and within a predetermined interval based on the collection time of the respective object data. Cross-validation techniques can then be used to evaluate the training of machine learning programs using the subject data. Further, cross-validation techniques may be used to retain data provided by a particular source (e.g., vehicle 102 and/or user) and then compare the entered candidate tags 136 in the retained object data to the results of training the machine learning program. Then, if the comparison indicates that the object data set includes a rejected label, e.g., the source includes an incorrect label for the object based on the results of training the machine learning program from other object data, the server 128 may reject the label as deemed incorrect. Rejected labels may be removed from object data that will later be used to train a machine learning program.

Further, the server 128 may generate a classification for the subject data source (e.g., the user and/or the vehicle 102) based on accepting or rejecting tags in the subject data from the subject data source. The classification may be based on a score or rating for the object data source. For example, if the object data from a source includes a tag that is determined to be one of correct or incorrect, e.g., based on cross-validation, the server 128 may be programmed to update a classification, e.g., a rating, for the source. A rating in this context is a numerical value that may be used to assign a weight to be given to an input candidate tag 136 in object data from a source. The rating may indicate a confidence that the tag from the source will be accurate (i.e., match the ground truth). For example, the source may be initially assigned a default or normal value, such as 0.8 or 80%. The server 128 may then be programmed to adjust the default rating up or down when an incorrect or correct tag is deemed to have been provided. Further, the server 128 may be programmed to adjust the default rating up or down after considering that the total number of incorrect or correct tags have been provided from the source. The total number of correct or incorrect tags may have to exceed a threshold number, e.g., 10 tags, 100 tags, etc., and may be determined by assigning a positive value to the correct tag and a negative value to the incorrect tag and then determining the total number as the sum of the values assigned to the correct and incorrect tags.

The user's rating may be used to provide a reward to the user, e.g., tokens or the like may be provided to the user device for purchase, discounts, or the like. The rating may also be used to provide an incentive to the user for improvement to receive rewards. Further, the computer 104 of the server 128 may provide the updated data collection module 122 to the vehicle 102 by adjusting the rules for requesting user input based on the results of the cross-validation (e.g., based on adjusting the rating of the subject data source (e.g., the vehicle 102 or a user of the vehicle 102)). For example, a classification of the object data source based on the rating may specify candidate tags 136 that allow or disallow the user to provide input. The updated rules in the data collection module 122 may specify that a user who was previously allowed to provide a candidate tag 136 for input is no longer allowed to provide a candidate tag 136 for input and/or that a candidate tag 136 input by the user will be ignored, e.g., not provided in the object data from the vehicle 102 to the remote server 128.

Further, a classification of an object data source, such as a user, may include a rating of the source for a particular type of object. The type of object means a classification of the object that can be output by the machine learning program, e.g., vehicle 102, rocks, road signs, pedestrians, bicycles, fences, etc. are the type of object. The computer of the server 128 may be programmed to determine the type of one of the objects in the object dataset, for example, according to a machine learning program. Based on the identified type of the object from the machine learning program and the cross-validation of the identification of the type of the object in the object dataset from the source, the rules in the data collection module 122 may be updated to specify the frequency (e.g., on a scale of zero to one, where zero is "never" and one is "always") that a user of a candidate tag 136 requesting input to be provided to one of the objects when the candidate tag 136 specifies the type.

In some implementations, the computer of the server 128 may be programmed to compare the input candidate tag 136 in the corresponding set of object data to map data to perform a verification of one of the input candidate tag 136 or the map data. As described above, the object data generally includes position data specifying a position at which an image included in the object data is collected. The location in the object data may be compared to a location specified on the map to verify the entered candidate tag 136. If the location in the object data is within a predetermined threshold of the location of the object specified on the map and the input candidate tag 136 identifies the type of object indicated for the location of the object specified on the map, such as a landmark, traffic light, etc., it may be determined that the input candidate tag 136 has been verified. Thus, the comparison of the input candidate tags 136 to the map data may be used to improve the tags used to train the detection module 124, and/or may be an alternative or additional mechanism to the cross-validation described above for adjusting the ratings of the object sources.

As described above, the detection module 124 can be used to provide output to operate one or more vehicle subsystems 110, including various components, such as the braking subsystem 112, the propulsion subsystem 114, the steering subsystem 116, and the HMI 118 of the vehicle 102. The braking subsystem 112 resists movement of the vehicle 102, thereby slowing and/or stopping the vehicle 102. The braking subsystem 112 may include friction brakes, such as disc brakes, drum brakes, band brakes, etc.; a regenerative brake; any other suitable type of brake; or a combination thereof. The braking subsystem 112 communicates with and receives input from the computer 104 and/or a human operator. A human operator may control the braking subsystem 112 via, for example, a brake pedal. The steering subsystem 116 controls the rotation of the wheels. The steering subsystem 116 communicates with and receives input from the steering wheel and/or the computer 104. The steering subsystem 116 may include a rack and pinion system with electric power steering, a steer-by-wire system (such as is known, for example), or any other suitable system. Propulsion subsystem 114 may include one or more of an internal combustion engine, an electric motor, a hybrid engine, and the like.

Fig. 2 and 3 show respective examples of the HMI 118 in the vehicle 102 that includes a candidate object 132 surrounded by a bounding box 134 and a set of candidate tags 136 for the candidate object 132. While the collection module 122 in the vehicle 102 is executing, the collection module 122 receives data from the vehicle 102 sensors 108, which is input to a machine learning program in the collection module 122, which then outputs the candidate 132 and a bounding box 134 for the candidate 132. In some implementations, the machine learning program in the collection module also outputs one or more candidate tags that can be included in the HMI for selection and/or confirmation by a user in the vehicle 102.

Fig. 4 is a block diagram of an exemplary deep neural network or DNN 138. For example, DNN 138 may be a software program that may be loaded into memory and executed by a processor included in computer 104. In an exemplary implementation, DNN 138 may include, but is not limited to, convolutional DNN 138 (CNN), R-CNN (region-based CNN), fast R-CNN, and faster R-CNN. DNN 138 includes a plurality of nodes, and the nodes are arranged such that DNN 138 includes an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. Each layer of DNN 138 may include a plurality of nodes. Although three hidden layers are shown, it is understood that DNN 138 may include more or fewer hidden layers. The input layer and the output layer may also include more than one node.

Nodes are sometimes referred to as artificial neurons 140 because they are designed to emulate biological (e.g., human) neurons. A set of inputs (represented by arrows) to each neuron 140 are each multiplied by a corresponding weight. The weighted inputs may then be summed in an input function to provide a net input, possibly adjusted by an offset. The net input may then be provided to an activation function, which in turn provides an output for the connected neuron 140. The activation function may be any suitable function, typically selected based on empirical analysis. As indicated by the arrows in the figure, the neuron 140 output may then be provided for inclusion in a set of inputs for one or more neurons 140 in the next layer.

As one example, the DNN 138 may be trained with ground truth data (i.e., data about real-world conditions or states). For example, the DNN 138 may be trained with ground truth data and/or updated with additional data. For example, the weights may be initialized by using a gaussian distribution, and the deviation of each node may be set to zero. Training DNN 138 may include updating weights and biases via suitable techniques, such as back-propagation and optimization. Ground truth data refers to data that is considered to represent a real-world environment (e.g., conditions and/or objects in the environment). Thus, the ground truth data may include sensor data that depicts the environment (e.g., objects in the environment), as well as one or more tags that describe the environment (e.g., tags that describe the objects). The ground truth data may also include or be specified by metadata such as one or more locations at which the ground truth data was obtained, a time at which the ground truth data was obtained, and the like.

In this context, the first machine learning program included in the collection module 122 may be a DNN 138 trained with ground truth data tags to specify real world objects, such as cars, trucks, trees, signposts, traffic lights, and the like. DNN 138 may be trained to output candidate object 132 and bounding box 134 of candidate object 132 and one or more candidate labels 136. For example, the DNN 138 may be trained to identify possible objects in the image of the vehicle 102 environment based on pixels representing the objects and pixels representing the remainder of the vehicle 102 environment, e.g., using edge detection techniques or the like. Further, the DNN 138 may be trained to provide one or more preliminary classifications of objects, i.e., may be provided as one or more candidate labels 136.

The object data collected by the collection module 122, which includes the first machine learning procedure, may then be used to train a second machine learning procedure included in the detection module 124. For example, after the user inputs the candidate tag 136 in response to displaying an image including an object in the HMI 118 of the vehicle 102, the computer 104 of the vehicle 102 may then transmit object data including a portion of the image defined by the bounding box 134 (sometimes referred to as a "cropped" image) along with the selected candidate tag 136. The cropped image may then be an image provided to train a second machine learning program. Further, as described above, the object data may include other data, such as the location of the vehicle 102 at the time the image was captured, environmental data, and the like.

FIG. 5 is a process flow diagram of an exemplary process 150 for training and deploying the object detection module 124.

The process 150 may begin in block 152, where a first machine learning procedure (e.g., DNN 138) is trained to identify candidate objects 132 and associated bounding boxes 134, as described above.

Next, in block 154, the collection module 122 is deployed in one or more vehicles 102, typically tens, hundreds, or thousands of vehicles 102.

Next, in block 156, the object data collected from the collection module 122 deployed as described above is provided to and received in the remote server 128, for example, stored in the object database 130, which may be a relational database, a file system, or the like. The various vehicles 102 may provide the collected data at various times (e.g., when the wide area network 126 is accessible, when the vehicle 102 is near or in a service center, at predetermined times, etc.).

Next, in block 158, the detection module 124 may be generated and/or updated at the server 128. That is, as described above, the detection module 124 may include a second DNN 138 that is trained to detect (i.e., identify and/or classify) objects. The detection module 124DNN 138 may be trained using object data collected as described above.

Next, in block 160, the detection module 124 may be provided to one or more vehicles 102. It should be noted that although the vehicle 102 is shown in fig. 1 as including both the collection module 122 and the detection module 124, various vehicles 102 will likely, and even likely, include one, but not both, of the collection module 122 and the detection module 124.

In block 162, the input from the detection module 124 may be used to operate one or more vehicles 102, at least in part, with the vehicle 102 computer 104 to assist the vehicle 102 operation. For example, the detection module 124 may provide identification of the object, and the vehicle 102 computer 104 may then actuate the vehicle subsystem 110 based on the object identification or classification. For example, the computer 104 may cause the vehicle 102 to change speed or direction, i.e., actuate one or more of the braking subsystem 112, the propulsion subsystem 114, and the steering subsystem 116, in response to object recognition provided by the detection module 124.

After block 162, the process 150 ends.

Fig. 6 is a process flow diagram including details of an exemplary process 170 for executing the collection module 122 for training the object detection module 124 and training the object detection module.

The process 170 begins in block 172, where the collection module 122 in the vehicle 102 monitors the vehicle 102 environment of the candidate 132. As described above, the collection module 122 may include a first machine learning procedure to detect the candidate object 132. The collection module 122 may also include programming for initiating monitoring, for example, when the ignition of the vehicle 102 is in an "on" state, when the vehicle 102 is moving, when the collection module 122 is activated according to user input, when the collection module 122 is activated based on the GPS sensor of the vehicle 102 specifying that the vehicle 102 is in a location in the area that the collection module 122 is programmed to monitor, and so forth. The collection module 122 may also include the following programming: when the candidate object 132 and bounding box 134 are output by the machine learning program in the collection module 122, the images of the candidate object 132 and bounding box 134 are displayed and possibly also the candidate label 136 of the candidate image.

Next, in block 174, the computer 104 of the vehicle 102 may determine whether the collection module 122 has output the candidate 132. If so, block 176 is performed next. Otherwise, process 170 proceeds to block 180.

In block 176, the computer 104 may cause the candidate object 132 and the associated bounding box 134 to be displayed in a display of the HMI 118 of the vehicle 102, for example, as shown in fig. 2 and 3.

Next, in block 178, the computer 104 may receive input providing the candidate tag 136, for example, via the HMI 118 of the vehicle 102. For example, the user may select candidate tag 136 from the list provided as shown in fig. 2 and 3. Alternatively or additionally, the computer 104 may be programmed to accept the candidate tag 136 specified by the user without one or more suggestive lists of tags. That is, the list of candidate tags 136 in fig. 2 and 3 may be omitted, or even if they are not limited, the user may provide an input, such as a voice input, specifying a tag (e.g., "car," "tree," "bicycle," etc.) regardless of the list of candidate tags 136.

After block 174 or 178, in block 180, it is determined whether the process 170 continues. For example, a user input may be provided to stop the process, the vehicle 102 may transition to an "off" state, and so on. If the process 170 is to continue, block 172 is next performed. Otherwise, process 170 proceeds to block 182.

In block 182, the object data collected and stored in block 178 is offloaded to server 128 (e.g., or stored in object database 130) for training detection module 124. As described above, the object data generally includes an image defined by a bounding box 134 that includes candidate object 132, as well as an input candidate tag 136 of the object, and possibly other data, such as environmental data. The object data may be offloaded from the vehicle 102 computer 104 via various mechanisms (e.g., via scheduled transmission over the wide area network 126, by accessing a data port on the vehicle 102, etc.).

After block 182, the process 170 ends.

The use of "responsive to," "based on," and "in determining \8230;" herein indicates causal relationships, not just temporal relationships.

According to the invention, a system is provided having: an image sensor having a field of view external to the vehicle; a human-machine interface (HMI) in the vehicle arranged to display an image based on data from the image sensor; and a first computer comprising a processor and a memory and programmed to: providing data from the image sensor to a machine learning program, the machine learning program outputting a bounding box around an object; causing the bounding box surrounding the object to be displayed via the HMI; and transmitting object data including the tag identifying the input of the object to a second computer remote from the vehicle.

According to an embodiment, the machine learning program further outputs one or more candidate tags for the object, and the first computer is programmed to receive input specifying a user selection of one of the one or more candidate tags.

According to an embodiment, the object is a first object of a plurality of objects and the bounding box is a first bounding box of a plurality of bounding boxes; the machine learning program further outputs the plurality of bounding boxes, including the first bounding box and at least one second bounding box; and further wherein each of the bounding boxes is provided around a respective object of the plurality of objects including the first object and at least one second object.

According to an embodiment, the object data further comprises data relating to the environment surrounding the vehicle associated with the time at which the input tag was input.

According to an embodiment, the data from the image sensor comprises a plurality of video frames comprising the object and captured within a time interval while the vehicle is moving.

According to an embodiment, the input tag is a first input tag and is associated with a first time in a time interval, and the object data comprises one or more second input tags respectively associated with one or more second times in the time interval.

According to an embodiment, the vehicle is a first vehicle of a plurality of vehicles and the object data is a first object data set of a plurality of object data sets, whereby the input tag is one of a plurality of input tags of the respective object data sets; and the system further comprises the second computer, wherein the second computer comprises a second processor and a second memory and is programmed to receive the plurality of object data sets from respective ones of the plurality of vehicles.

According to an embodiment, the second computer is further programmed to perform cross-validation to validate or reject tags in one or more of the object data sets.

According to an embodiment, the second computer is further programmed to remove rejected tags from the object data.

According to an embodiment, the second computer is further programmed to: providing an updated data collection program by adjusting rules for requesting user input based on results of the cross-validation; and providing the updated data collection program to the vehicle.

According to an embodiment, the second computer is further programmed to classify a user associated with one of the object datasets based on the results of the cross-validation; the rule specifies whether the user is allowed to provide input data; and adjusting the rule comprises determining that the user is not allowed to provide the entered data.

According to an embodiment, the second computer is further programmed to determine a type of one of the objects in the object data set; when a candidate tag specifies the type, the rule specifies a frequency of requesting input to be provided to a user of the one of the objects that provides the input tag; and adjusting the rules comprises adjusting the machine learning program to present the type of object more or less frequently to a user providing the input label based on a result of the cross-validation.

According to an embodiment, the second computer is further programmed to compare a respective input tag with map data to perform verification of one of the input tag or the map data.

According to an embodiment, the machine learning program is a first machine learning program and the second computer is further programmed to generate a second machine learning program based on the plurality of object data sets to perform object recognition.

According to an embodiment, the second computer is further programmed to provide the second machine learning program to one or more of the plurality of vehicles or another vehicle.

According to an embodiment, the first computer is further programmed to receive the second machine learning program and operate the vehicle according to the object recognition output from the second machine learning program.
